stories.body:
While world leaders prepare for annual UN gathering, shifts in the global order continue in the face of a disruptive American president

I n the event of a midterms election battering, it is possible that a deflated Donald Trump , constrained by a Democrat-controlled Congress, will gradually have to face up to the indignity of irrelevance.

While continuing to sign off Truth Social posts with his usual, “Thank you for your attention to this matter”, no one will actually be paying much attention. His meandering press conferences will no longer be carried live by TV networks. The Republican party will move on to the question of his successor. Trump could announce he had changed the name of the Champs-Élysées to Sunset Boulevard and even Google Maps will stifle a yawn. He would become that most pitied of political animals, the lame duck.

Yet somehow this scenario does not seem to fit the Trump personality, the US media landscape or indeed the recent history of other presidential endings. Just before completing their own terms in office, George W Bush launched the Iraq war “surge”, Bill Clinton got China into the World Trade Organization and Ronald Reagan helped end the cold war.

Trump will also surely rage against the dying of the light.

Many observers, including the former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton and the former UK foreign secretary David Lammy, predict Trump will concentrate even more on his disruptive foreign policy after November’s midterms, seeking to go even further and faster. Potential legislative gridlock in Congress would block him off from domestic initiatives, so the thinking goes, but much less so foreign policy.

The likes of António Guterres, attending his final UN general assembly as secretary general this week, who have tried to impress on Trump that the US could achieve more in alliance with others than alone, are likely to receive short shrift.

Those hoping for a return from the orderless world to one of order, loosely built around a set of recognisable values, are likely to be disappointed. In short, there is more to come.

T hat assessment is accelerating a trend across the world of countries forming a complex web of diplomatic, military and trading alliances designed to act as protective shields from an unpredictable and predatory US president. These hedging alliances, born out of fear of entrapment or of abandonment, are springing up across the globe, changing the matrix of diplomacy, often but not always in favour of the other superpower of the age, China.

John Bew, a foreign policy adviser to four former British prime ministers, describes the process as the creation of “a sub-threshold international order”.

As Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, urged in a speech at Davos in January, the middle powers are reorganising. The trend is most obvious among former US allies.

Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, said: “The world is moving from a situation where countries saw themselves within the context of an alliance system – ‘How do we plug and play and make it all about interoperability with American grand strategy?’ – towards one where the primary goal is: ’How do we hedge and how do we make sure that we can defend ourselves if America isn’t there?’”

Wherever one looks it is the alliances in which the US does not feature – from Brics to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) – that are thriving and deepening.

The recent Brics summit in Delhi ended with a declaration 140 dense paragraphs long that centred on how sovereign states can insulate their economies, supply lines, and payment infrastructures from weaponised western financial networks. The aim was to show that the “global south” can shape rules without turning into an anti-American alliance. “The operational strategy does not aim to eradicate the dollar overnight,” the Indian commentator Navroop Singh explained, “but to construct a parallel, non-dollar pipeline through which bilateral commerce, especially in strategic commodities like oil, gas, agriculture, and critical minerals can flow unhindered by extraterritorial oversight of the United States.”

At this month’s SCO meeting at Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan, China’s president, Xi Jinping, said: “The overwhelming majority of countries do not subscribe to power politics, do not want conflict and confrontation, and do not wish to remain closed off and left behind. Instead, they aspire to secure an equal place on the world stage through their own development and international cooperation.”

Formed to manage border disputes among former Soviet states, the SCO’s activities long ago expanded to include an economic dimension fostering connectivity, trade and investment.

By contrast, in the groupings that the US dominates, such as the G7 and Nato, the recent key ambition has been to shape an agenda that avoids a Trump walkout. Success is measured according to whether the west avoids public disintegration.

Sometimes these new ad hoc alliances are relatively mundane. Some operate inside existing institutions, others involve the creation of specific new cooperation trading mechanisms such as memorandums of understanding on trade in critical minerals or the development of new overlapping institutions. In the case of the UK, the Chatham House thinktank suggests as many as six different mini-alliances could be formed to build submarines and air engines, share critical minerals, or promote free trade.

The biggest and most striking recent manifestation of this new order came in the Middle East on 7 August, when Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca pact – a defensive military alliance that for some is about ending the dependency on the US military umbrella, and for others combatting Iran. Either way, it is likely to rewrite the Middle East’s security architecture.

Trita Parsi, from the US foreign policy thinktank the Quincy Institute For Responsible Statecraft, said: “If you sit in the Gulf Cooperation Council countries right now, you must feel tremendously vulnerable because you have put all your eggs in the American security basket and it turned out not only not to work, but it was supposed to be a guarantee that others would be deterred from attacking you. Instead, the US started a war against the wishes of most Gulf countries and within that war, the entire infrastructure of the US bases turned out not to be a deterrent, but a magnet.”

Not only were exposed bases pummelled by Iranian missiles and drones to the point, in the words of Gen David Petraeus, that they became “no longer viable”, the Gulf states also discovered the US was prepared to allow Israel to bomb Qatar’s capital, Doha, in the hope of assassinating the Hamas leadership. It was the first such attack on a GCC state, and changed the GCC’s security calculations as to whether Iran or Israel ultimately was the primary threat in the region.

The US insists in public it will reinvest in better-protected bases and will shortly lay out a postwar vision in which the US remains indispensable to the Gulf’s security. But Majed al-Ansari, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said: “Gulf nations cannot rely solely on the US and other international alliances for their security. Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward.”

Parsi admitted it was not clear what kind of tree would grow out of the seed sown in Mecca. “Is it another bloc formation that at its core divides the region, leading to rivalry and confrontation, or is it, as the Turks insist, an open constellation that is not targeting anyone but based on collective security?”

Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, meanwhile, requires foreign investment, tourism and reliable energy routes. Endless wars promoted by Israel and not constrained by the US for purposes not in Saudi Arabia’s long-term interest are a ball and chain on the Saudi economy.

In all this, there are deep implications for India, a country dependent on the Middle East for nearly 60% of its crude oil and about 70% of its liquefied natural gas requirements. It may need to form its own hard power security partnerships in the region.

Writing in Foreign Affairs magazine , Marc Lynch, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University, asked recently: “If Washington could not even be counted on to consult its allies, defeat its adversaries, or protect its partners from the fallout of its regional misadventures, then what good were its promises? The fundamental bargain the United States offered has crumbled, and it will not be easily rebuilt”.

The same set of questions has been posed in Europe, leading to calls for a more Europeanised Nato, most often perceived as an alliance of its five main military powers, a constellation that conveniently bypasses Brexit and would allow Germany, France, Italy, Poland and the UK to work together to face the Russian threat, assuming these democracies next year remain led by forces opposed to Putin’s authoritarianism.

Debate about this alliance, promoted at the Munich Security Conference, is driven by the twin fears of the hybrid war conducted by Moscow and the US plan to leave the conventional defence of Europe to the Europeans. Trumpites treat Europeans primarily as trade competitors and sometimes a civilisational threat, not allies. No one can assume that the US would come to Europe’s defence in the event of a Russian attack. Not surprisingly, Poland, the Baltics and Scandinavia have since 2022 increased their defence spending by 71%, 134% and 126% respectively. The call to buy European arms is growing.

Such is the concern about where Trump could go next after his threats to Greenland, that some European diplomats privately express relief that the US was unable to repeat the success of Venezuela in Iran. There is no love for the Iranian government, save for its ability to remind Europe of the risks inherent in relying on US military and technological supremacy.

T he country that most acutely faces the American dilemma is of course Canada . Now entering an asymmetric trade war with the largest and most powerful country in the world, it has little doubt about the rupture it is confronting. Bob Rae, a former Canadian ambassador to the UN, recently wrote: “Canada’s nextdoor neighbour is a predatory hegemon [that] tears up treaties, makes a mockery of international law and clearly has a different concept of the relationships between might and right, and between law, morality and self-interest.”

But there was an ambiguity deep in Carney’s Davos message. Was he seeking simply to locate new markets blocked by US tariffs, or was he trying to build a network of countries – a third bloc – with like-minded liberal values? Rae argued that for the middle nations alliance to thrive, Carney needed to be clearer about what values Canada stands for, including upholding international law. He wrote: “We can succeed in defeating such aggression only if we are willing to extend economic, political and military support to other countries and jurisdictions facing similar attacks and threats.”

In his speech to the European parliament this week while trying to provide the cure to the harsh realities his Davos speech diagnosed, Carney argued that associate membership of the EU would not just be about economics, but an affinity of deep-rooted shared values that implicitly Canada no longer shared with the US. But the rules-based EU does not give access to its markets readily, and the big vision could soon become entangled in the small print Brussels adores.

Sometimes this crisis of the west is seen as an exclusively European phenomenon. But South Korea finds itself in a similar place to Canada. Ulchi Freedom Shield, the annual joint military exercise that the US and South Korea held to counter the North Korean threat, was abruptly scaled back by Washington just before it was due to begin in August. Trump ordered the drills cut from 11 days to five, citing costs, his desire to improve relations with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, and South Korea’s reluctance to support his war on Iran. The decline in US military stocks due to the Iran war has hardly helped.

It has intensified a debate in South Korea , and in Japan, about pursuing independent nuclear weapons, especially given the apparent indifference of the US and the international community to North Korea’s programme.

The friction has given Xi a golden opportunity to promote China to South Korea and Asia as the more reliable ally.

Optimists such as Kurt Campbell, who under Joe Biden’s presidency latterly as deputy secretary of state did more than anyone to reconstruct American alliances across Asia after the Trump first term, insists his task can be repeated. There is no need to panic, he said, arguing that “by the winter there will be a dramatic resurgence in discussion, debate, hope and, frankly, optimism about what comes next”. The old centrifugal forces including European aversion to Chinese protectionism and US dominance in artificial intelligence, will resurface.

The counterview is that something fundamental has changed. Once bitten, twice shy, the old transatlantic order will not be restored, and something new, less predictable, more fragmented is already taking shape.

stories.title: Nvidia’s free AI model could push the UAE closer to the U.S.
stories.summary: The Emirates owns the machines but rents the intelligence. Nvidia’s next free AI model could change that.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Innovation

The Emirates owns the machines but rents the intelligence. Nvidia’s next free AI model could change that.

Nvidia’s chips are driving the United Arab Emirates’ rise as an artificial-intelligence power. Next on offer is free software, a model built to rival China’s best.

Last month, Nvidia spent $7 billion to buy a stake in U.S. coding startup Poolside and license the tools it uses to build AI models. The new model is due by the end of the year for anyone to download for free, and it is aimed at buyers already running Nvidia hardware, Marc Einstein, an analyst at Counterpoint Research, told Rest of World . Few countries fit that description better than the UAE, whose flagship data center will run on 400,000 Nvidia chips .

For years the UAE positioned itself as neutral ground between the U.S. and China, buying chips from the former and, until recently, equipment from the latter. It built its own free model, Falcon, to avoid relying on imported software. That neutrality has been fading since G42, the state-backed AI company, cut its Chinese ties to win Nvidia’s chips. It would narrow further if the country also opts for the new model.

“The last missing piece was the model layer,” Mohammed Soliman, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a foreign-policy think tank in Washington, told Rest of World . “Nvidia already owns the chips. Now it is scaling the factory that produces the models that run on those chips, and it is releasing them as open weights.”

Build or rent?

The two institutions leading the UAE’s AI push each have their own view on whether to build sovereign AI models from scratch or lean on existing technology from other companies.

The Technology Innovation Institute, the government lab behind Falcon, insists on building its own models from the ground up, while G42, which runs the UAE’s AI infrastructure, has aligned itself with Nvidia’s push for free models.

The value is not limited to the models we ultimately produce, but it lies in mastering the underlying technology and retaining control.” Hakim Hacid, chief researcher, Technology Innovation Institute

“As a model-building lab, we believe that maintaining diversity in AI perspectives, and preserving full technological sovereignty, requires a strong, homegrown foundation,” Hakim Hacid, TII’s chief researcher, told Rest of World . “The value is not limited to the models we ultimately produce, but it lies in mastering the underlying technology and retaining control across the entire AI stack.”

G42 did not answer Rest of World ’s questions about whether it would use Nvidia’s model. The company has been an early supporter of Nvidia’s push to give away powerful models. In July, Nvidia formed an alliance around the argument that countries need AI models they can inspect and control, and G42 joined immediately, becoming the only Gulf company to do so.

“Frontier open models are an essential part of that future, alongside frontier closed models, with security, trust and sovereign control designed in from the start rather than bolted on later,” G42’s CEO, Peng Xiao, wrote on X at the time.

Building on someone else’s model need not mean giving up control, Soliman said. Sovereignty in AI is a matter of degree rather than an all-or-nothing choice, he said.

“Sovereignty was never about inventing the foundational model from scratch,” Soliman said. “It is about the model’s weights, how you fine-tune the data, and, most importantly at this stage, your ability to serve these models to users in the UAE and other markets.”

The U.S. government approved sales of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to the UAE after G42 sold its stakes in Chinese technology companies two years ago. In July, it placed the UAE in the group of countries it treats as its closest technology allies. The software running on those chips is mostly rented from U.S. companies, which decide what the models may do and who may use them.

Falcon was meant to be the exception. TII built it in 2023 as a free alternative to models from the U.S. and China, and it ranked first this year on Counterpoint’s index of state-backed models.

Saudi Arabia, which is competing with the UAE to become the region’s AI hub, has taken a different route. Humain, the state AI company, is cleared to buy tens of thousands of Nvidia chips, and introduced an Arabic model this month that it had commissioned from a Chinese lab. A year earlier, it had launched one it said was built from scratch in the kingdom.

“It shows there’s little full-stack lock-in: The Saudis are using Chinese AI models to build their own models, while using U.S. chips to develop and run them,” Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow at the think tank Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told Rest of World . “These states have strong incentives to hedge and will continue to do so for as long as they can.”

Nvidia’s Nemotron

Nvidia has its own reasons for wanting countries to take the upcoming model, expected to be called Nemotron 4.

Earlier versions of U.S. AI models have lagged well behind China’s free models, which were downloaded roughly 2 billion times this year, far ahead of any Western rival, according to an August report by Hugging Face, the platform where developers share and download AI models.

To change that, Nvidia has also agreed to pay almost $13 billion to buy Hugging Face . Governments building their own models mostly start from a free one made by Meta or Alibaba, and Nvidia’s spending is meant to make Nemotron the base they pick instead, Einstein said.

The Poolside deal “appears less about displacing incumbent model families and more about increasing future adoption of Nemotron within an ecosystem where Nvidia already has a strong hardware position,” Einstein said.

TII says it can do both. While the foundation stays Emirati, anything better from elsewhere can still be put to work, Hacid said.

“Sovereignty does not mean isolation,” he said. “We build our foundation at home, while remaining open to the best of the world.”

Additional reporting by Divsha Bhat in Dubai.

Where in the world is the iPhone cheapest?

Apple’s high-end models cost more in markets like India and Turkey owing to high taxes and import duties.

The AI talent war is coming for Big Tech’s Asia executives

OpenAI and Anthropic are hiring leaders from Meta, Google, Microsoft, and other U.S. tech giants to win new markets across India and Southeast Asia.

The case for a robot tax to redistribute wealth

In an excerpt from his book, “Innovate for Impact: A Roadmap to Sustainable Technology Beyond AI,” Alessandro Crimi explains that a tax on automation is more effective than retraining labor.

stories.title: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit
stories.summary: Top US and Chinese officials held talks in New York on Sunday ahead of a Trump-Xi summit this week.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met China's Vice Premier He Lifeng

Published 9 hours ago

Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday.

Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York.

The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week.

AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks.

He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade.

A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November.

The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI.

Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people."

The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries.

In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears abouts its potential negative impact on humanity.

Trump has largely dismissed those concerns , arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China.

He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins."

In May, when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing, ways to collaborate on AI was one of the issues the two leaders discussed.

Those talks ended with an agreement that China would buy Boeing jets and US agricultural goods in exchange for lower tariffs.

Unions, thinktanks and others say overhaul could provide investment Britain needs

Unions, thinktanks, environmental groups and charities have come together to call on ministers to boost the financial firepower of the national wealth fund to empower it to invest more in Britain and rebalance the country’s economy.

Lower energy bills, the revitalisation of the UK’s industrial heartlands and the provision of more high-quality jobs could all be unlocked by scaling up the NWF, according to a statement from organisations including the TUC, Greenpeace , WWF and the New Economics Foundation.

The statement calls on the government to overhaul the NWF by turning it into a “world-leading national development bank capable of delivering the investment Britain needs”, while insisting this would be consistent with the government’s existing fiscal rules .

The NWF was launched in July 2024 by the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, with the aim of attracting billions of pounds of private sector money for large infrastructure projects.

It was a manifesto promise and aimed to attract a mix of investment – roughly £3 of private funds sought for every £1 of taxpayer cash in schemes such as ports, gigafactories and hydrogen and steel projects.

The NWF is not a sovereign wealth fund, such as those owned by Norway and Saudi Arabia, which manage cash generated by the government through state-owned natural sources such as oil, and surpluses from international trade, bank reserves or privatisation projects.

Instead, it is designed to boost investment in key industries while giving investors the confidence to park money in the UK by showing the government is willing to share the financial risk of large infrastructure projects.

The call to expand its scope comes just before the Labour party gathers for its first conference since Andy Burnham became prime minister and as John Healey draws up his first budget as chancellor , scheduled for 28 October.

The group’s statement praises the “important role” played by the NWF in “steering private investment to support clean energy, modern infrastructure and regional growth – for example, through its £500m partnership with the Manchester Good Growth Fund”.

However, it calls on such public banks to do more, comparing the £5.5bn available for the NWF to invest each year for the next five years with the €62bn (£53.5bn) lent by Germany’s public investment bank KfW to households, businesses and municipalities in 2025 alone, almost 10 times higher.

The statement lays out several ways a scaled-up NWF could benefit Britain, including:

Turbocharging the retrofitting of homes and buildings.

Giving the public a bigger stake in critical infrastructure through taking part-ownership stakes in key projects.

Launching a targeted investment programme to bring new green industries to communities hit hardest by deindustrialisation.

Supporting a network of regional banks to funnel money into the small businesses that hold up local economies.

after newsletter promotion

This would require the government giving the NWF independence to raise its own finances and invest over the long term, the group said, a practice followed by other public banks around the world.

The group said this move would be consistent with the government’s fiscal rules – where ministers match day-to-day spending with their income and only borrow to invest – and would combine “fiscal credibility with economic ambition, delivering visible investment”.

Burnham has said since entering Downing Street that he would look at “any flexibility” within the government’s existing fiscal rules to help borrow billions more to invest in infrastructure.

A Treasury spokesperson said the NWF had delivered £3.9bn of investments in its first year in projects such as Sizewell C and a second gigafactory in Sunderland, as well as boosting flood defences in Wales. They added that an additional £5.25bn had been generated in private finance, while 11,500 jobs had been secured and created.

The spokesperson said: “The government remains committed to the NWF’s long-term mission to crowd in private capital and drive economic growth into every postcode in the country.”

stories.title: Helen Jenner unveiled by Nigel Farage as new leader of Reform in Wales
stories.summary: Farage says it was "untenable" for former leader Dan Thomas to continue after his arrest last week.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Farage described Jenner as a "determined campaigner" and "someone I trust"

Published 21 September 2026, 12:02 BST

Nigel Farage has unveiled Helen Jenner as the newly-elected leader of Reform in Wales, replacing Dan Thomas after his arrest on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Speaking on the steps of the Senedd in Cardiff on Monday, Farage said: "I've known Helen for many, many years. She is a determined campaigner."

Farage said he felt sorry about former leader Thomas's "personal difficulties" and that it had been untenable for him to continue, adding: "We could have done without this bump in the road."

Jenner, who served as Thomas's deputy alongside her role as Senedd member for Bangor Conwy Môn, said it was an honour to be elected to the top job.

A leadership vote was held by Reform's 33 Senedd members on Monday morning, and Jenner confirmed that her colleague Jason O'Connell had stood against her.

O'Connell had not been expected to stand, and there had been no vote of the wider party membership.

Speaking to reporters outside the Senedd, Farage said there would be a vote for a new Welsh deputy leader to replace Jenner on Tuesday.

Dan Thomas steered Reform to its best-ever result in a Senedd election in May, becoming the second-largest party in Wales

Jenner had been interim leader and favourite to replace Thomas, with sources telling BBC Wales that "very senior" Reform figures had backed her.

She is a married mother-of-two from Anglesey and had spent 15 years working as a teacher.

A fluent Welsh speaker, Jenner had been a member of all Farage's parties since UKIP, and stood for the Brexit Party in the 2019 Senedd election.

For the first time all of the Senedd's group leaders now come from north Wales, with two from the island of Anglesey where Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth is also from.

An arrest, a defection and a new leader - how Reform's 'challenging' week unfolded Published 1 day ago

Reform's ex-Welsh leader Thomas stepped down on 15 September after his arrest on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. He was bailed pending further enquiries , and denies doing anything wrong.

He was not on the steps of the Senedd for Jenner's unveiling as leader, but he had been among the Reform Senedd members who met in Cardiff Bay last week to discuss their next steps, with a party official from London attending to oversee proceedings.

Farage said that it had been "pretty much untenable for him to continue as leader".

He said Jenner was "someone I trust".

Farage said the party will carry on "as if nothing had happened, waiting for Dan, who is going to stay a member of this place, to come back more actively with us".

Farage told BBC Wales he was happy for Thomas to continue as a Reform MS while the investigation continues.

"He hasn't been charged for anything," he said.

"We're going to crack on being a voice of opposition here in Cardiff. We're going to crack on being really active when it's in session, and we're going to crack on getting ready to fight 1,200 council seats which come up all across Wales for local government next month."

Jenner said the last week had been a "really difficult time" for the party

Jenner told BBC Wales there were a "few things" Reform needed to change, including giving members more of a say on policy.

"We've done an excellent job of holding the Welsh government to account so far," she said.

"We've gained consensus across the chamber on some issues and we've really held them to account".

She denied the party had a "unity issue" after James Evans claimed last week he would have had "majority" support to stand as leader had he not ruled himself out.

"I think that it was a really difficult time for us," Jenner said of the last week.

"But I think we are really united in terms of what we're trying to achieve here."

The news that Thomas had resigned as leader coincided with the separate decision by Reform's Sarah Cooper-Lesadd to defect to Plaid Cymru .

Farage said he could "not tell you what is going on in the mind of Sarah Cooper-Lesadd" and that her defection "just doesn't make any sense".

A Welsh Labour spokesperson said: "Just months after the Senedd election, Reform has already seen its leader resign and one of its members leave the party. Alongside departures from its council groups in England, that raises serious questions about its stability and ability to deliver for the people it represents."

stories.title: EU Kids Act Won't Keep the Internet Accountable and Trustworthy
stories.summary: The EU Commission draft law to restrict young people’s access to the internet that it presented last week will come at a high cost: it will put online services behind age gates, expand the use of intrusive age verification, and undermine the privacy of all users. The EU Kids Act aims to protect children from risks associated with social media, video games, and AI systems by introducing age-based access rules, safety requirements, and stronger enforcement and oversight measures. It presents itself as building on the Digital Services Act (DSA) and puts into “hard law” some of the safety-by-design measures specified in the non-binding DSA guidelines on minors’ protection. The proposal is built around the following elements: social media age “delay”, safety by design, age assurance and parental responsibility, and strong enforcement. Each of these measures are concerning. Mandatory Age Gates for Social Media and Video-Sharing Platforms Following the advice of an expert panel , the proposal would create a phased access to social media and video-sharing platforms deemed risky—a threshold met simply by relying on personalized recommender systems or offering “uninterrupted content consumption”: no service accounts for children under 13; restricted accounts under tight parental supervision from 13 to 15; and autonomous accounts in a safe-by-design environment from 15 to 18. Full online access is therefore reserved for adults. However they’re designed, age gates undermine civil liberties, reduce safety, and create barriers to internet entry, often at the expense of marginalized groups. If this sounds complex and like a compliance nightmare, that’s because it is. The access delay comes with privacy-intrusive age verification across the board, relying on the EU age verification scheme. For teenagers, this law means significant control in the hands of their parents, who must set up accounts and prove that they are, in fact, parents, adding yet another problematic layer of verification. stories.body:
The EU Commission draft law to restrict young people’s access to the internet that it presented last week will come at a high cost: it will put online services behind age gates, expand the use of intrusive age verification, and undermine the privacy of all users.

The EU Kids Act aims to protect children from risks associated with social media, video games, and AI systems by introducing age-based access rules, safety requirements, and stronger enforcement and oversight measures. It presents itself as building on the Digital Services Act (DSA) and puts into “hard law” some of the safety-by-design measures specified in the non-binding DSA guidelines on minors’ protection.

The proposal is built around the following elements: social media age “delay”, safety by design, age assurance and parental responsibility, and strong enforcement. Each of these measures are concerning.

Mandatory Age Gates for Social Media and Video-Sharing Platforms

Following the advice of an expert panel , the proposal would create a phased access to social media and video-sharing platforms deemed risky—a threshold met simply by relying on personalized recommender systems or offering “uninterrupted content consumption”: no service accounts for children under 13; restricted accounts under tight parental supervision from 13 to 15; and autonomous accounts in a safe-by-design environment from 15 to 18. Full online access is therefore reserved for adults.

However they’re designed, age gates undermine civil liberties, reduce safety, and create barriers to internet entry, often at the expense of marginalized groups.

If this sounds complex and like a compliance nightmare, that’s because it is. The access delay comes with privacy-intrusive age verification across the board, relying on the EU age verification scheme. For teenagers, this law means significant control in the hands of their parents, who must set up accounts and prove that they are, in fact, parents, adding yet another problematic layer of verification.

In fairness, the Kids Act’s gradual approach at least appears to be designed with some proportionality considerations, rather than imposing a blanket social media ban. J ust last month a French court declared such undifferentiated bans unconstitutional. The EU Kids Act distinguishes between age groups and certain services and follows a risk-based approach. This means, for example, that age verification is not required for existing accounts if the provider can tell with a “high degree of confidence” that the user is above the age threshold—a vaguely specified standard.

Yet, the law still indiscriminately covers social media and video-sharing, with virtually all mainstream services being covered by the proposal. The broad scope also sits uneasy with the use of age thresholds, which remain a blunt proxy for maturity. What is more, by focusing heavily on safety and harms, the EU Kids Act pays little attention to the privacy and freedom of expression rights of users, as well as the right of children themselves to access information and to participate online. However they’re designed, age gates undermine civil liberties, reduce safety, and create barriers to internet entry , often at the expense of marginalized groups . They also create a powerful infrastructure for control and further entrench the power of big tech.

The proposal exempts not-for-profit encyclopedias, scientific repositories and educational services, as well as open-source software-developing and-sharing platforms. However, no exceptions are foreseen for small and medium-sized enterprises, which will only foster the dominance of resource-laden tech companies that were already investing in similar measures. And we know that most companies are well-advised to play it safe and use privacy-unfriendly age checks across their platforms.

Safety by Design Across Covered Services

The proposal’s second pillar, “safety by design”, casts a wider net. It applies across social media, video-sharing, online games, AI companions, chatbots and even app stores—with varying requirements. Providers must generally make child-safe design the default and can relax from the requirements only if they use age assurance to establish that the user is an adult.

For example, rules on addictive features such as infinite scrolling, safe account settings, and more choice over recommender systems are to provide a safe internet experience to young people. As regards AI companions and chatbots, the proposal requires companies to design their services to reduce minors’ exposure to emotional dependencies and harmful interactions. Online games are covered as well: they must come with contact protections. The law also makes app stores the gate keeper for age-appropriate access, based on an age-rating system.

The devil of these measures lies in the details, but all of them raise fundamental rights concerns and some of them seem poorly suited, if at all, to the decentralized architecture of the Fediverse. The requirement for very large online platforms to set up compliance plans before rolling out new services raises additional questions about the risks of transplanting product-safety doctrines of conformity and risk control into speech regulation. Deciding what is “safe” can easily become a question of what content people can access or share.

Next Steps

By choosing to regulate all these aspects through the Kids Act, the Commission not only but creates a privacy minefield, it also intermingles the digital fairness agenda with the more fundamental-rights heavy questions of age assurance and access to information. An unfortunate policy choice that will politicize well-intentioned efforts to curb manipulative and addictive design practices (read our position on the DFA ).

It speaks volume that the Kids Act has not gone through a full impact assessment process, which would typically require a systemic check of alternative policy options and stakeholder consultations. Looking forward, we call on the EU lawmakers to pull the teeth of the most harmful suggestions and to make sure that the new measures don’t erode the fundamental rights of all users.

stories.title: Googlebooks launch October 4 starting at $899—here are the five models you can preorder today
stories.summary: Googlebooks offer premium hardware and deep smartphone integration, but you may not like the price.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Googlebooks offer premium hardware and deep smartphone integration, but you may not like the price.

Google is ready to take a swing at laptops… again. The company has had a lot of success in phones, but it has struggled to parlay that into an effective strategy for larger screens. Chromebooks have been fine as a budget option, but it seems like Google has accepted they’ll never compete with macOS or Windows. That’s where Googlebooks come in. These new Android-powered laptops are intended to be “real” computers, featuring premium hardware, on-device apps, and powerful development tools.

After the Googlebook reveal at I/O this year , Google’s partners are now ready to sell you one. The first Googlebooks are available from several OEMs that have been making Chromebooks over the years, but don’t expect Chromebook pricing. There’s only one model under a grand, and the rest are well above that.

Familiar hardware

The bulk of Chromebooks have been budget machines, and they looked the part. Googlebooks, however, feature bright OLED screens, metal builds, big haptic trackpads, and the Glowbar. All the machines have this illuminated bar on the lid, but it doesn’t do much for now. It lights up when the device boots and can display battery level, but Google says it’s going to release an API for developers to add more features.

Across the full lineup, Google says you can expect 16GB of RAM with 32GB upgrades for some models. At launch, the machines will run either a Snapdragon X Elite or an Intel Core Ultra Series 3 (Panther Lake) chip. Both platforms have an NPU capable of 45 TOPS of on-device AI performance, and all the designs are fanless. Regardless of the exact model, Google says you can expect up to 14 hours of video playback and 16 hours of web browsing.

Here are all the launch models and their starting prices.

The Acer model is the cheapest, and it’s also the only convertible in the lineup. The price jump from that device to the next cheapest (the Dell XPS) is a substantial $300, and the rest of the launch laptops are $100 more than that. Google’s partners launched a few Chromebooks in this price range, but they didn’t see wide adoption.

The apps you know but bigger

A major part of Chrome’s failure to truly compete with macOS and Windows is down to software availability. Google tried multiple ways to shoehorn local apps into its web-first platform, but it never took. The advantage of starting from scratch, according to Google, is that these new laptops share the same software stack as Android phones. That means you can run Android apps natively without all the VM weirdness of ChromeOS, and there are a ton of those.

Google is aware of the sordid history of running phone apps on desktop PCs. It’s often a clunky experience using a phone app designed for touch on a large screen with a keyboard and mouse, but the company claims you may be surprised how many apps in the Play Store are now optimized for laptops. The Play Store client will call out apps and games that have been optimized for bigger displays, and Google says more apps are being updated for laptops all the time. There will also be a “desktop-class” version of the Chrome browser preinstalled on Googlebooks.

Even if optimized, these are still going to be apps designed for, and primarily used on, smartphones. It’s unclear if they’ll offer the kind of power people expect for a $1,300 laptop. On the gaming side, Google notes that its Level Up program is delivering more experiences suitable for a keyboard and mouse, but the selection of desktop-ready games won’t be anything like what you get on Windows or macOS.

There is, of course, nothing stopping you from using phone apps on a Googlebook if you want. They’ll run in a window, and you may not even need to install them. With Cast My Apps, the apps installed on your Android phone are available instantly on a Googlebook. They appear in a dedicated app list on the laptop, allowing you to open and use them without touching the phone. The file manager can also seamlessly access files on your Android phone.

Similarly, a feature called Continue On lets you pick up where you were in a phone app on the Googlebook version of the app. This requires developer support, so not all apps will carry over. Still, this level of integration with Android is not something you get on either Windows or macOS, which could make a Googlebook appealing if you’ve got a Pixel or Galaxy riding around in your pocket.

As you would expect, the Play Store is the primary source of apps for Googlebooks, and there will be some limits on sideloading. Google has confirmed to Ars that Googlebooks will enforce developer verification requirements for apps similar to Android phones. Under this system, only apps from developers who have verified their identities with Google will be eligible for installation from a downloaded APK file. This requirement will roll out broadly next year, but it’s being activated in a few markets in the coming weeks .

The AI play

Google is following through on its promise to make AI a core part of the Googlebook experience. Gemini models are going to be deeply integrated with the software, ready to work on your screen context with a cursor wiggle. Google calls this Magic Pointer, and it has a few suggestions about how to use it.

Let’s say you have an email or PDF with dates you need to add to your calendar. You can jiggle the cursor, point Gemini at the email, and get all the dates added in one go. If you get a suspicious email, you can invoke Gemini with your cursor and ask it to figure out if it’s a scam. You can also point Gemini at images and tell it to edit them or generate new versions without downloading anything. Useful? Maybe occasionally, but Google’s enthusiasm for Magic Pointer seems a bit premature.

Rambler, the AI-powered voice input tool that debuted on Pixel 11 phones a few weeks ago, will also be included on Googlebooks. That means you can start talking to fill text in any field with streamlined instant editing to remove “ums” and corrections. On phones, I’ve found this can make your writing voice sound like a sterile AI output, but if you’re just banging out a quick email, maybe that’s fine for most people.

AI-powered development is also a big part of the Googlebook experience. Devices will come with Antigravity, allowing you to task agents with development work. You can build, test, and even deploy apps right on your Googlebook, which might help fill some of the software gaps. For more serious developers, there will also be a full terminal environment for tools like Claude CLI and Antigravity CLI.

Nth time’s the charm?

The initial OEM Googlebook lineup looks nice enough—you might not be able to tell them apart from a premium Windows laptop at a glance, but this is a completely different animal. You’re relying on Google to follow through on its promise to make Android apps work for a large-screen environment, which has been a problem in the past. If Google can’t get developers to produce powerful desktop-class apps for Googlebooks, it’s going to be hard to justify buying one over Windows or macOS.

Google’s focus on Googlebooks as an Android companion makes sense given the shared software foundation, but it’s also a risky play. These are not cheap devices—by Google’s own admission, it’s going after the premium laptop market. While Android accounts for about half the phones across Googlebook launch markets, Google’s OS has a much smaller share of the premium segment (over $600) compared to Apple. People buying more expensive phones might also consider a high-end laptop like a Googlebook, but there’s little reason for iPhone owners to buy one of these in a world where the MacBook Air is around the same price, and the MacBook Neo is even cheaper.

Preorders for the five launch models are going live today, and they will be on shelves on October 4 in the US. Launch day is October 5 in Canada, the UK, Ireland, France, Germany, and Australia. Devices will be available from the Google Store, Best Buy, and other “select retailers.” All Googlebooks, even the cheapest $899 model, will come with a year of Google AI Pro, offering expanded Gemini usage limits and 5TB of Google Drive storage. All models will also include a year of GeForce Now for game streaming.

If you decide to order one of these laptops, you’ll have to go in somewhat blind. No one outside of Google and its OEM partners has spent considerable time using these devices, and we don’t expect anybody to have one for testing until launch day.

On Friday, MeToo journalist Sophia Huang Xueqin was released from prison. She returns to a landscape changed by censorship, and a new generation of feminists

W hen Jasmine, a once active member of China’s MeToo movement, organises feminist activities in Beijing, she often does so under the guise of an art or cultural event. She avoids publicising them on social media, instead sharing details privately in her personal circle.

It’s very difficult to imagine what happened during the MeToo period, she says, “when one survivor could speak publicly about her experience and trigger a broader discussion about sexual harassment.”

On Friday Sophia Huang Xueqin the imprisoned journalist who helped to ignite China’s MeToo movement, was released from prison, five years after her arrest. She will return to see a feminist movement that has dramatically changed in the years she has been detained.

In China feminism has become an increasingly private affair. Activists speak of a generational rupture. A movement once inspired by the global hashtag campaign against sexual abuse and harassment has retreated to a less public space.

Across Chinese social media survivors post about sexual harassment and successful court cases online. But activists say hashtag campaigns like MeToo and its Chinese language equivalents have largely been scrubbed from the Chinese internet.

“A lot of younger, digital-native feminists today don’t know much about those earlier feminist struggles not too long ago, thanks to the state’s intentional annihilation of them,” says Eva Liu, a researcher on Chinese feminism and digital media at Ohio University.

Today, Chinese feminists employ creative ways to avoid censorship. They use new expressions to avoid posts being blocked. “It’s really a cat-and-mouse game,” says Liu.

She describes an “encyclopaedia” of feminist words banned by Chinese censors. “There are staff specifically tasked with tracking new terms coined by feminists online and adding them to the keyword lists used for automated censorship,” she says. “Even some terms that are not yet popular among feminist users are already part of this automatic censorship list.”

Li Sipan, a Chinese investigative journalist and feminist scholar, says: “The Chinese Communist party regards all mobilisation of the public and movements demanding changes from the government as threats. The feminist movement clearly has these characteristics.”

Jasmine in Beijing says: “If you want to organise a public event, anything explicitly related to feminism or LGBT issues is basically not possible, at least in Beijing. If you advertise it that way, there’s a risk the event will be shut down.

“So usually we frame the event in a more neutral way, without directly presenting it as being about gender or social issues. But once the event is taking place, we may still discuss those topics.”

‘The online environment now is very different’

Huang’s reporting of survivors’ stories helped to propel the MeToo movement into public consciousness in China. She was arrested in 2021 in the city of Guangzhou a day before she was set to leave China to study a masters degree at Sussex University on a UK government-funded scholarship.

In 2024 she was convicted alongside labour activist Wang Jianbing of “inciting subversion of state power”.

Huang’s friends say they received little information about her from the authorities while she was in detention, amid reports of dramatic weight loss and intense interrogation, resulting in little sleep. Information travelled slowly out of the prison. They sometimes waited months for updates, relying on messages from other inmates who had been released.

At the time of her conviction, Huang was also sentenced to four years “deprivation of political rights”. Human right groups say it could prevent her from continuing to work as a journalist or travelling abroad.

In a statement released on Saturday, activists pushing for Huang’s release said “though she is released from prison, none of us [her friends] were able to reach her or receive any information from her.

“Her whereabouts is also unknown. We are nervous and worried about her current conditions due to the potential severe surveillance she faces.”

The Chinese government says the country has made “historic” progress in women’s rights. In a speech last year, president Xi Jinping listed improvements in health, employment and economic participation. China says it will further strengthen gender equality and protect against sexual harassment and sexual violence.

Despite the shrinking space for debate, activists say the movement has had a lasting impact on Chinese society. Metoo made sexual harassment a mainstream topic. It led to policy change in universities, although activists say progress stopped at the courts.

“I believe the achievements of China’s MeToo are things that many other authoritarian or even democratic countries failed to achieve,” says Lu Pin, a Chinese feminist activist, based in New York. “Under very harsh conditions, MeToo greatly raised women’s awareness of their rights, especially among young women.”

In Beijing, Jasmine hopes to meet Huang one day but is unsure if it will be possible. She says she is still in contact with survivors of sexual harassment and believes it’s possible to support them with publicity and legal support.

She believes there are other individuals and groups offering similar help, but they must choose carefully how to effect change. “The online environment now is very different from when MeToo first emerged,” she says.

Lu Pin agrees. “People used to have naive imaginations and expectations about the internet, but later realised it wasn’t like that, especially for women and feminism.”

stories.title: Tories pledge to bring back tax-free shopping for tourists
stories.summary: The party says scrapping the scheme in 2021 left the UK less competitive than European destinations.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch (left) and shadow culture secretary Rebecca Paul visited Bicester Village, a designer outlet shopping centre popular with tourists, to promote the policy

Published 4 hours ago

The Conservative Party has pledged to bring back tax-free shopping for tourists from outside the European Union.

The Tories said the decision to scrap the scheme in 2021 left the UK less competitive than European destinations.

Leader Kemi Badenoch, who was a Treasury minister when the tax relief was abolished, said businesses were being "let down by a tax policy that is chasing their customers away".

But Labour accused the party of "a spectacular U-turn".

The VAT Retail Export Scheme - which allowed overseas visitors to get a VAT refund on items they had bought in Great Britain and took home in their luggage - was scrapped for non-EU visitors under the previous Conservative government in 2021, while it was also not extended for EU visitors.

At the time, Badenoch said it was "a costly relief which does not benefit the whole of GB equally".

However, the Conservatives have now set out plans to restore VAT refunds for eligible visitors from outside the EU.

The party said that if evidence confirms the scheme "pays its way", this would be extended to visitors from the EU by the end of the next Parliament.

It said the cost of reintroducing the scheme would be offset by cracking down on "NHS health tourism", including more consistent charging of patients ineligible for free treatment, minimum recovery targets for debts and requiring full repayment of debts before visa applications or renewals will be considered.

The remaining costs would be funded from a package of savings set out by the Tories last year.

Reinstate VAT-free tourist shopping, businesses say Published 7 September 2023

Bring back duty-free perk to boost London - mayor Published 2 February 2023

The party also argued the move would benefit shops, hotels, restaurants and the wider tourism industry.

It pointed to research by the Centre for Economics and Business Research (Cebr), which suggested fully restoring tax-free shopping for tourists could attract up to 2.35 million extra visitors and generate £4.1bn in extra spending.

The report from earlier this month also estimated that for every £1 of VAT refunded, this could generate £1.54 in other taxes.

Badenoch said: "We have iconic retailers, inventive designers and brilliant manufacturers, but they are being let down by a tax policy that is chasing their customers away.

"Holidaymakers are choosing rival cities in other countries for the simple reason that it saves them money."

Businesses have long called for tax-free shopping for tourists to be reintroduced, arguing they are at a disadvantage to other European countries.

EU countries offer VAT refunds for non-EU visitors, while other European countries such as Switzerland have similar schemes.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive at the British Retail Consortium, said: "Introducing a modern tax-free shopping scheme would help attract more international spending to the UK, supporting high streets, jobs and investment in towns and cities across the country.

"Done properly, it would boost economic growth and deliver a net benefit to the Exchequer."

However, a Labour spokesperson said: "Kemi Badenoch used to say tax-free shopping was a costly giveaway and now she's trying to sell it as an economic miracle.

"If they really think it's such a great idea, they should explain why they scrapped it in the first place and how they'd pay for bringing it back."

stories.title: EFF Statement on California Governor's Executive Order on AI
stories.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom's executive order is an opportunity for a needed, thoughtful conversation about artificial intelligence and its potential harms. Everyday Californians are feeling real anxiety about the risks of artificial intelligence, and as an organization that works to ensure technology empowers people, EFF welcomes this order as a way for the state of California to lead a much-needed dialogue that addresses these concerns. Nonetheless, the most immediate and current concerns with this technology are not about sci-fi scenarios concerning rogue super-intelligence. They are happening right now through biased algorithmic decision-making for employment or government benefits , AI-powered surveillance systems such as Flock cameras , and artificially inflated personalized pricing . People want state and federal leaders to act, and we urge Gov. Newsom to develop thoughtful policies to address those concerns. Today’s EO is a good start. To that end, EFF supports the focus on expanding the reporting requirements under SB 53 (2025) for loss-of-control incidents, alongside third-party investigations. We urge the administration to consider how to make these third-party investigations available for smaller developers. As the Government Operations Agency prepares its recommendations for the governor, we urge leaders to also realize that the effectiveness of kill switches in advanced AI systems remains an area of active research. As such, they should ensure that - as we’ve previously mentioned - any technology regulation targeting cybersecurity practices at AI labs must be careful, precise, and practical . Moreover, we also caution that government-controlled kill switches run the risk of being used as a form of retaliation against protected speech, as demonstrated by the Trump Administration’s retaliatory actions against Anthropic earlier this year. Ultimately, true safety requires California to focus on concrete, immediate, and urgent harms of AI technologies by ensuring that algorithmic decision-making in both the government and private sectors respects people’s rights and well-being. We urge Gov. Newsom and the state of California to develop thoughtful policy in collaboration with those most at risk of harm to address these and other concerns.

stories.title: Silent Hill: Townfall review – shame and suffering on the Scottish coast
stories.summary: PlayStation 5, PC; Screen Burn Tragedy, and an apocalyptic fog, befall a fishing community. It is up to outsider Simon to offer some kind of closure You spend a considerable portion of Silent Hill: Townfall in a kind of foetal position, cowering behind objects that will be eerily familiar to anyone who lived in the UK during the 1990s. Cars seem to be modelled on the era’s boxy Volkswagen Golfs; logos adorning phone boxes should narrowly escape the attention of copyright lawyers at BT Group. (For millennials, the deja vu will likely intensify the horror, as if stepping back into a childhood nightmare.) Simon, the nerdy, unassuming star of the game, pokes his head around corners to catch a glimpse of the demonic entities that wish to maim him, before shrinking back down again with a downwards motion of the analogue stick. In such moments, it’s easy to imagine him wrapping his arms around his knees, clasping his eyes shut and wishing himself away from this place. The game’s setting, St Amelia, is based on the fishing communities of the East Neuk of Fife. The terror lurking here is wonderfully specific: absent lairds, island poverty, an oil-drilling corporation. Anguished beasts lumber down quaint streets lined with sandstone houses and fluttering bunting. This venerable horror series may have shifted to Scotland, yet we remain firmly in classic Silent Hill territory – weather and all. St Amelia finds itself suffused in supernatural fog and the vast majority of its inhabitants have vanished following some kind of mass tragedy. The artful, evocative presentation is such that you can almost taste the in-game air, the briny seaside tang diluted by rainy mist. Continue reading...

stories.title: Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘Why aren’t these companies being held to account?’
stories.summary: After a week of alarming warnings about artificial intelligence’s potential to destroy the world as we know it, our technology reporters answered your questions on the reality of the AI threat IcommentthereforeIam asks: Given our senses, emotions, memory and moods, is it ever going to be accepted that humanly conscious AI is fantasy? Dan: This is a serious question that has even rattled Richard Dawkins, the evolutionary biologist. He may not believe that God is real but he does believe that AI is conscious - or at least the chatbot he was using, which he called Claudia. “You may not know you are conscious, but you bloody well are,” he wrote. And he’s not the first. In 2022 Google fired an engineer who went public with his belief that a company-developed AI had feelings. At the more troubling end of this belief, there are countless examples of people becoming overly attached to, and influenced by, AI chatbots – including cases of psychosis. Aisha: There’s certainly a theatrical – even “psy-op” - quality to the flurry of AI doomsaying over the past weeks. It’s hard to say entirely what concrete developments are at the root of it all. We know that the Hugging Face incident , where a “swarm” of AI agents hacked another company, has been one trigger of the drama. There have been other contributing incidents too – Dario Amodei suggests internal developments at Anthropic have prompted his latest round of blogging, and there’s been some X discourse and doomy muttering about bioweapons. We aren’t in the heads of Dario Amodei or Sam Altman, and so we cannot say how sincere they are, and how much they might have other goals in mind – such as, perhaps, delaying their IPOs until their finances look better. But any company of their size, and with their potential liabilities, would be angling hard to be regulated as favourably as possible. That’s what big companies do. Continue reading...

Next month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, one of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said, while adding she did not expect the prime minister’s previous disparaging comments about the US president to be an issue.

Burnham is expected to meet Trump early next week at the UN general assembly summit in New York, the pair having previously spoken twice by phone since Burnham entered No 10.

As Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham said Trump would not be welcome in the city, saying also that UK politicians who indulged him “should be ashamed”.

Asked about the comments, Bridget Phillipson , the Labour chair and minister for women and equalities, told Sky News: “Look, I think what you’ve just described there is politics. The president knows that. This is far from unique.

“People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.”

She nonetheless repeated UK condemnation of Trump’s on-and-off military campaign against Iran, which has disrupted global oil supplies, causing significant inflationary pressures , saying this would make life more difficult for John Healey, the chancellor, as he plans the budget.

The economy was, Phillipson said, “in a strong position”, especially with growth figures.

She said: “But that’s not to take away from the very real challenges that you identify, particularly where it’s come to the conflict we’ve seen in the Middle East and the impact that that’s been having on businesses and on families close to home.

“We took the decision not to involve ourselves in that conflict. That was the right call. The US will take their own foreign policy decisions, but I believe, and still believe now, it was the right decision for us as a country not to get involved in that conflict. Of course, something that, had Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage been running the country, we would have jumped headlong into a conflict with it without end.

“And yet, and we do see the consequences here at home and as we go into the budget, making sure that we are doing everything we can to give people that breathing space to tackle those challenges around the cost of living has been at the forefront of everything that Andy Burnham has done since becoming prime minister.

“I know it’s at the forefront of the chancellor’s mind as he’s planning for that budget later on next month.”

after newsletter promotion

In a later interview with the BBC, Phillipson was dismissive of comments by Jim Ratcliffe, the petrochemicals billionaire, who said this week he had lost confidence in the UK due to levels of immigration and taxation.

She said: “You’ll forgive me if I do take with a pinch of salt what someone who is a tax exile has to say about our country.” Ratcliffe is resident for tax in Monaco.

Burnham has previously defended his comments about Trump in a similar way, saying of the US president: “Well, he’s said things as well, and everyone says things as politicians. In the moment, you meet people where they’re at, and you find a connection with people, and that’s always been my style.”

With the wider UK-US relationship, there were “differences of opinion”, Phillipson said, while arguing that Burnham could see beyond those differences with Trump in maintaining invaluable ties.

She said: “We don’t have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one president, any one prime minister.

“It’s something that has stood the test of time over many centuries, despite political differences. They come and go. What matters most is the British national interest. And that’s what Andy Burnham will deliver for our country.”

stories.summary: It joins Great British Railways as part of government plans to save money and improve services.

stories.body:
Chiltern Railways, which was privatised in 1996, has become part of the Great British Railways

Published 20 September 2026

Chiltern Railways has been brought into public ownership after 30 years as a private company.

It is the 10th rail company now under the Great British Railways (GBR), the government's programme of public ownership , which it says will save money and improve services.

Chiltern Railways, which was privatised in 1996, operates services from London Marylebone to Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Warwickshire, as well as destinations in the West Midlands.

The government said the transfer into public ownership would tackle overcrowding by introducing 25 additional daily services from December.

The start of the first day of public ownership saw some disruption, with Chiltern warning the line between Birmingham and Marylebone , external was "expected to be much busier" due to the late notice of the West Coast Main Line closure affecting services at London Euston.

The operator said it would run more trains than usual between the stations with significantly enhanced capacity.

The Department for Transport (DfT) said the additional weekday services under GBR would provide 10,000 extra seats.

They would include half hourly services during weekdays on the Chiltern Main Line between London and Birmingham, as well as more weekend services.

Rail minister Lord Peter Hendy met staff at Marylebone Station on Thursday alongside the first Chiltern train in the GBR livery.

"The most difficult thing on Chiltern is that it's shorter capacity and those extra trains and those extra seats will make a real difference to people travelling on this line up here from Marylebone every day," he said.

Rail minister Lord Peter Hendy said the government hoped to "build a railway the country can trust and rely on"

The rollout of the new trains would also improve accessibility and provide better Wi-Fi on board, the rail operator said.

From Sunday, passengers whose train had been cancelled can use another operator's service two hours either side of their train to get to their destination at no extra cost, it added.

Chiltern's interim managing director Tony Baxter said: "Sunday is a significant milestone for Chiltern Railways and we look forward to working together with the wider rail industry to deliver a better railway for everyone in Great Britain."

The aim is for GBR to operate all passenger services by the end of 2027.

Great Western Railway's services will be the next operator to be brought into public ownership, on 13 December.

Lord Henry said: "Every transfer into public ownership gives us the chance to tackle the bread-and-butter issues people care about – more frequent, comfortable trains that turn up on time.

"As we set up Great British Railways (GBR), we're putting passengers first.

"It will not happen overnight, but we will build a railway the country can trust and rely on and that will create growth, jobs and homes."

stories.body:
In case you missed it, Rachel Cusk’s new novel Life of M has been the centre of heated online debate. Dubbed a “biogossip” (biography based on gossip) allegedly inspired by the actress Natalie Portman, the novel investigates fame, power and truth with a particular emphasis on storytelling.

Much of the discussion of the book revolves around the similarities between Portman’s real life rather than how Cusk explores her chosen themes. In a recent article for The Guardian , journalist Elle Hunt provides a handy list of must-know information for those wishing to read the novel but may be unsure of all the details. The biogossip argument is certainly plausible. For instance, references to Léon: The Professional (1994) and Black Swan (2010) are easy enough to pick up if you are aware of Portman’s filmography. At the conclusion, Hunt asks whether more gossip in literature could solve the crisis of people reading less than ever.

It is interesting to consider whether easy-to-spot references to public figures are the key to drawing new readers in. However, asking for more gossip may be addressing the symptoms rather than the cause and ignores the fact that gossip has always existed in literature, and to a far greater extent than you might think.

Since the birth of the modern novel, scandalous discourse has permeated stories in complex and exciting ways. The genre of the biogossip has existed since the 1600s , with French writer Madeleine de Scudéry credited with writing the first roman à clef (French for “novel with a key”). Stories within this genre satirise current affairs, placing real figures behind thinly veiled character disguises.

These books were a way of discussing controversial topics and sharing insider knowledge while avoiding charges of libel. Take de Scudéry’s novel Artamène ou le Grand Cyrus (co-written with her brother Georges) discusses major figures associated with The Fronde (1648 to 1653), a series of uprisings against the regency government of Queen Anne of Austria and her chief minister, Cardinal Mazarin. Using ancient Persia as a veil for 17th-century French court dynamics, de Scudéry contributed her tuppence-worth via the ten volume novel.

But liking gossip and being a good gossiper goes much further when it comes to reading.

Consider the last time you had a really good gossip session with a close friend, going over an incident in excruciating detail. It feels like a simple thing to engage with when, in reality, complex social processes are occurring simultaneously.

Gossip relies on individuals holding knowledge about a social network, and the quality of the conversation is dependent on the extent to which participants engage with the information being evaluated. It is expected that you offer an opinion, which not only contributes to the communal knowledge pot but is also a demonstration of a your morals, perceptions and assumptions . We are not always conscious of this happening, but we usually walk away from a conversation with a better understanding of other people and ourselves – how we react to certain behaviours, actions and motivations.

The same process can be applied to literature. Regardless of genre or era, novels naturally rely on characters interacting with their fictional contexts, including social networks. The intimacies and power dynamics navigated through a novel can be decoded by using the same skills we exercise when we gossip.

Every conversation a reader is privy to in a novel is essential to the practice, as it is the author providing breadcrumbs that lead to deeper character insights. Their reactions and responses inform our understanding of what the novel is trying to do. By engaging with the text in the same way we gossip, it unlocks a channel through which classics and other supposedly inaccessible texts can be understood.

Take, for example, the first page of Pride and Prejudice . Austen deploys gossip to illustrate the Bennett parents’ attitude to marriage: Mrs Bennett has heard from Mrs Long that Netherfield is to be occupied by a young eligble man, which only excites the local mothers. Mr Bennett remains unmoved, he’s even disparaging of the prospect of one of his girls marrying the handsome, single, rich landowner. Mrs Bennett’s desperation to get her girls married versus her husband’s lax attitude hints at the forthcoming conflicts of the novel. Eagle-eyed readers can notice this and unlock how Austen is satirising marriage culture from the opening lines.

Read more: Jane Austen’s world ran on gossip – and she revelled in it

The same can be applied to Shakespeare plays. Much Ado About Nothing is in essence a series of carefully constructed gossip that relies on the subject of conversation to be within earshot and so generating the plot and moments of character development.

The play’s subplot involves Don Pedro, Ursula and Hero playing matchmakers for Benedick and Beatrice. Don Pedro’s gang carefully arrange a conversation in which Benedick overhears them gossiping about Beatrice’s unrelenting affection for him. Likewise, Ursula and Hero ensure Beatrice is present for their gossip about Benedick’s affections for her. The result? They confess their love for each other and the subplot is resolved – all thanks to the power of gossip.

So, what does that mean for readers? It is generally understood that fictional stories are excellent ways to wrestle with what it means to be human and all the messy parts that go with it. By reading as a gossip, we specifically practice the identification of behavioural signs and patterns and can apply the knowledge to future scenarios, both fictional and non-fictional.

In the process of gossip, we become better at reading social situations because we have an insight into the potential subtexts of any given conversation. It also makes reading more enjoyable and helps illuminate the similarities between someone from the 18th century and us in the present. It unveils the persistence of humanity’s problems, from awkward interactions to first loves, and helps us realise that we are not alone in our experiences.

I invite you to pick up a book and keep an eye out for any gossip – you might just find out something new.
